content: Health and non-health programs should be integrated to achieve comprehensive development outcomes. HIV programs must be incorporated into broader health initiatives and data recording and reporting systems. National programs should define a core package of high-impact HIV interventions that span prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care services. These interventions should be included in the national health benefit package and funded, at least partially, through the national health financing system. The package must be tailored to different populations, locations, and settings, and it should be reviewed and updated regularly. A minimum data set with prioritized metrics to measure service utilization and outcomes is essential for building stronger, more efficient, and effective health information systems to support the HIV response. Since immediate funding and implementation of all interventions and services may not be feasible, a phased approach should be adopted. This involves progressively introducing essential interventions, expanding the range of services offered, increasing population coverage, and reducing out-of-pocket expenses for users. The recommendations in these guidelines must be considered within the context of the full spectrum of HIV interventions and services, as well as the overall national health benefit package. In countries with dedicated national HIV budgets, priorities must be set across all HIV interventions. In the absence of such budgets, the prioritization of HIV interventions must be considered alongside all essential health interventions. Clear criteria are needed to guide decision-making within the range of HIV interventions and services and for the broader national health benefit package. A structured framework is provided to address implementation considerations based on program needs and available resources. This framework includes principles, processes, strategic information, objectives, context, priority selection, quantification, costing, monitoring, evaluation, strategic planning, funding applications, implementation, and reprogramming. The ultimate goal of these guidelines is to achieve and sustain universal coverage of services with the greatest impact on the epidemic. Countries are encouraged to set ambitious targets and strive to meet them, while addressing disparities in service coverage, capacity limitations, resource constraints, and quality concerns through phased or sequenced implementation. Sequencing should ensure that the implementation of each recommendation builds on the previous one to achieve sustained scale-up and high-quality services. Analytical tools are available to assist in planning, including estimating the potential impact and costs of implementing new recommendations. Tools such as Spectrum, OneHealth, and Optima HIV are available for free and can support decision-making, costing, and resource allocation for HIV interventions. These tools provide insights into the impact of interventions on reducing HIV transmission, AIDS-related deaths, and treatment needs, as well as optimizing resource allocation to achieve defined objectives. The AIDS Epidemic Model (AEM) is another tool that reflects key subpopulations and transmission modes driving concentrated HIV epidemics. It uses epidemiological, behavioral, and programmatic data to model historical trends and project future scenarios based on behavioral changes or programmatic inputs. This guideline will be evaluated to assess the uptake of its recommendations into national policies and programs, with data made available through the WHO country intelligence database. A public health approach to HIV treatment focuses on addressing the health needs of populations rather than individual cases. This approach ensures broad access to high-quality services through simplified and standardized methods, balancing the best-proven standards of care with feasibility in resource-limited settings. Key elements include simplified drug formularies, fixed-dose combinations for first-line treatment, free care and drugs at the point of service delivery, decentralized and integrated services, task sharing, and standardized clinical monitoring. Acute HIV infection refers to the period between initial infection and the detectability of HIV antibodies. Acquired HIV drug resistance develops when viral mutations emerge during replication in individuals receiving antiretroviral (ARV) drugs. Adherence refers to the extent to which a person follows agreed recommendations from a healthcare provider, such as taking medication or changing lifestyle behaviors. Advanced HIV disease in adults, adolescents, and children aged five years and older is defined as a CD4 cell count below 200 cells/mm³ or a WHO clinical stage 3 or 4 event at presentation for care. All children under five years living with HIV are considered to have advanced disease. Age groups are defined as follows: adults are older than 19 years, adolescents are 10–19 years, children are 1–9 years, and infants are younger than one year. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) involves using a combination of ARV drugs to treat HIV infection. Combination prevention refers to integrating behavioral, biomedical, and structural approaches to maximize the impact on reducing HIV transmission and acquisition. Community health workers are trained individuals who provide standardized health services outside formal medical curricula. Differentiated service delivery adapts HIV services to better meet the needs of people living with HIV while optimizing health system resources. Integrated health services ensure a continuum of care, including health promotion, disease prevention, diagnosis, treatment, management, rehabilitation, and palliative care, tailored to individual needs throughout the life course. Key populations at high risk of HIV include men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, prisoners, sex workers, and transgender individuals. These groups often face legal and social challenges that increase their vulnerability to HIV and create barriers to accessing health services. Lay providers are individuals trained to deliver specific healthcare services without formal professional certification. Low-level viraemia refers to detectable viral load results between 50 and 1,000 copies/ml. Midwives are healthcare workers who have completed recognized midwifery education programs. Non-physician clinicians are professional healthcare workers capable of performing many diagnostic and clinical functions of physicians but are not formally trained as physicians.
